newsitem.title: USA: Credit card delinquencies rise in fourth quarter.
newsitem.headline: Credit card delinquencies rise in fourth quarter.

text.p: As concern grows about mounting U.S. credit card debt, new evidence emerged Thursday that consumers are having difficulty managing their borrowings.

In the fourth quarter of 1996, late payments jumped to 3.72 percent of credit card accounts, the American Bankers Association said, the highest rate since it began tracking delinquencies in 1980 and up from 3.34 percent in the same period in 1995.
In the third quarter a seasonally adjusted 3.48 percent of accounts had late payments, the ABA said.

Some regulators have sought to assuage concerns about mounting consumer debt by pointing to banks tightening standards for approving credit card applications. But in the fourth quarter of 1996, only 37 percent of banks reported tightening standards, a drop from 49 percent in both the second and third quarters of 1996, the association said.

"We are disappointed that the numbers didn't improve," ABA chief economist James Chessen said. "We had hoped that banks' tightening of credit standards over the last several years would have reversed the trend of delinquencies by now."

Delinquency rates also ticked up on home equity loans. The delinquency rate was 1.42 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, compared with 1.29 percent in the previous quarter and 1.41 percent in the same period the previous year.
On auto loans, the delinquency rate was 2.03 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, compared with 1.95 percent the previous quarter and 1.87 percent a year earlier.
Delinquent payments are defined as 30 days or more overdue based on the total number of loans outstanding.
